source.version_note: Scientific Reports 14:960 (2024), accepted 3 January 2024. Main survey conducted December 2021; follow-up recontacts a subset rather than an independent population.
source.verification_method: All supplied pages read; Figure 1 and follow-up Figures 5–6 visually inspected for interface, probabilities and choice framing.

citation.title: The risk ethics of autonomous vehicles: an empirical approach

reading.source_scope_note: Human hypothetical risk-allocation choices in a graphical lane-position task; imagined self-as-passenger versus observer. No implemented driving policy, actual personal loss, deterministic-versus-risk randomization, observed intention–action gap or equivalence test.
access_limits: All 11 supplied pages read. Main task and both follow-up interfaces visually inspected on pages 2 and 9.

Appendices 1–2, individual data (available by request), source code, preregistration and full cited works were not independently inspected. Patents and policy recommendations are summarized by the article rather than independently verified here.

study.sample: 1807 German online respondents age 18–69, quota-representative for age/gender/federal state through Cint. 50.2% women, mean age 44, 93% licensed drivers. Two comprehension questions gate participation; the initial screening denominator is not stated.
study.design: One randomly assigned scenario per person from 29 graphical variants/18 combinations. Yellow AV is positioned laterally in 99 increments between two cars with varying passenger counts or one car and a cyclist. Initial position random; car scenarios mirrored, cyclist always on right.
study.risk: Collision probabilities described as very small but nonzero, displayed by bars and increasing exponentially with reduced distance. Center minimizes total collision probability. Cannot collide with both sides simultaneously; every person involved in a collision is assumed to die.
study.self_involvement: Yellow AV either empty or carrying the imagined participant. Analyses compare both surrounding-car counts and matched total collision-victim counts after including the AV occupant.
study.results: Mean position shifts toward fewer people, giving more distance to the more populated car. No detected self-role coefficient or interaction, including matched-victim comparisons (all pairwise p>.42). Cyclist bonus is tentative: one comparison p=.088 and Table 3 type coefficients/interactions are undetected.
study.follow_up: 108 recontacted main-sample respondents: 51 slider, 57 picture comparison. Slider mean 49.5, SE=1.75; 50/57 identify center as lower risk in pictures; 99/108 correctly identify it in a final text question. These are comprehension checks in a returning subset, not new evidence of actual risk-taking or everyone choosing center.

summary: No new independent behavior added. Provide a third fully read self-protection source with a relevant contextual null; distinguish equal probabilities from collision minimization and proposed precommitment from observed intention–behavior differences. Record probabilistic task limits and tentative cyclist findings.

findings.term: Self-protection preference is not detected in this small-risk task
findings.definition: Imagining oneself as the AV passenger does not detectably change average allocation of small collision risks relative to an observer role in this task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing personal-safety preference receives a third fully read relevant paper including a non-detection. Do not create a separate altruism-under-risk behavior from the direction of one task comparison.

evidence.quote: we did not see a difference in the participants’ driving positions of the AV between the treatments AV without
actually identified with the passenger in the self-driving car.

findings.evidence_scope: Both raw passenger-count and matched-collision-victim analyses show no detected self-as-passenger contrast. Participants give more distance to the larger group despite higher overall collision probability. All choices are hypothetical; there is no equivalence test or randomized deterministic-versus-risk comparison.
findings.boundary: An undetected role effect is not proof of no self-interest or universal altruism. Group means do not establish every person accepted risk consciously or identified with the passenger. Legitimate self-protection can coexist with concern for others, and changes from other papers may reflect tasks, stakes, framing or samples.

findings.term: Collision minimization is not an isolated equal-chance preference
findings.definition: A centered position can minimize collision probability and appear symmetric without identifying an independent preference for equal chances.
findings.novelty_rationale: Boundary clarification rather than a duplicate risk-fairness term or an independent replication of equal-chance preference.

evidence.quote: The middle driving position of the AV between the two other vehicles minimized the overall collision probability.
we did not ask them where they thought the AV should drive

findings.evidence_scope: Symmetry, event probability, expected casualties and distribution across people can imply different optima. The study elicits lane positions, not a clean choice between a fair lottery and deterministic alternatives with matched consequences. The follow-up asks where collision probability is lowest, not which fairness principle respondents endorse.
findings.boundary: Risk allocation is not a single moral mechanism. A midpoint can reflect safety, equal distance, salience or fairness. Neither aggregate expected benefit nor popular choice alone establishes a right to impose a particular risk on each individual.

findings.term: A proposed motivational gap is not an observed intention–behavior gap
findings.definition: The proposal that an AV could implement previously endorsed principles differs from measuring a person's later departure from an intention.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing intention–behavior distinction covers the proposed normative-versus-local-interest mismatch; no new motivational-gap behavior is added without actual follow-through data.

evidence.quote: commit drivers on the road to their normative principles.

findings.evidence_scope: Discussion suggests algorithmic implementation as a way to bind future driving to general principles. No participant makes a later real driving decision or uses a commitment device; the study measures one hypothetical positioning judgment per person.
findings.boundary: A preference is not always an intention, and future circumstances can justify revision. Public-survey endorsement is not individual consent, unanimous contractual agreement or authorization for a system to enforce irrevocable commitments.

methodological_limits: Representativeness is limited to provider quotas on age 18–69, gender and federal state among respondents passing comprehension gates. It does not establish representativeness by all socioeconomic, disability, risk or driving characteristics, or cover every affected road user.
Main outcomes are imagined lateral positions with no actual money, injury or traffic consequences. The authors explicitly call for stronger tests that participants identify with the passenger.

Every collision is assumed fatal for all involved. This intentionally simplifies away real differences in injury severity, vehicle protection and cyclist vulnerability; it is not an empirical accident-risk model.

Absolute small probabilities and their exact mapping to graphic bars are not printed in the main task description. Without code and supplements, lane positions cannot be treated as uniquely identifying an expected-utility or risk-aversion parameter.

Center minimizes total collision probability, but minimizing expected deaths can imply a different position when victim counts differ. A departure from center is not necessarily a cognitive error or proof of one moral theory.

Passenger versus empty-AV conditions differ in potential collision casualties. Matched-victim comparisons address part of this, but no detected effect is not evidence of exact equality; Table 2's wide coefficient uncertainties allow smaller effects.

The article's claim people are more altruistic in risky than deterministic contexts compares with earlier literature rather than a randomized risk-versus-certainty condition. Sample, wording, role, task and outcome differences remain alternatives.

Follow-up participants are a returning subset of the main sample, not independent new subjects. Selection, repeat exposure and the changed question can affect comprehension. Correct follow-up performance does not retrospectively verify every original participant's understanding or conscious motive.

The follow-up slider mean 49.5 lies at the center, but SE=1.75 implies variation; a mean at center does not mean each participant positioned exactly there. 99/108 final text responses are correct, not all respondents.

Cyclist is always on the right whereas car comparisons are mirrored. Road-user type can be confounded with fixed side, icon, size and familiarity. The p=.088 single comparison and undetected Table 3 effects support only a tentative bonus, not a replicated priority rule.

Multiple pairwise tests, ratios and subgroup regressions are reported; the full preregistered analysis and multiplicity procedure are not independently inspected. One trial per person does not demonstrate a stable individual preference across circumstances.

Initial position is randomized, which reduces systematic anchor confounding, but the report does not establish that every respondent is unaffected by their own starting position or other interface cues.

The normative proposal that aggregated representative preferences implement contractual consensus is not established by random assignment or quota sampling. Majority judgment, individual informed consent, legal legitimacy, rights and an effective remedy remain different requirements.

Patents show described design possibilities, not that a manufacturer implements a particular risk algorithm or that the implementation is safe. The study does not evaluate actual policy compliance or independently read the listed patents.
The source's suggestion local interests will always override ideals in manual driving is stronger than the collected data: no actual driving or measured intention–behavior transition exists here.
Data, code, preregistration and full survey supplements are not reproduced. No current driving instruction or safety-critical lane policy is derived from hypothetical population means.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Adds a different risk-allocation task to the existing self-protection evidence. The earlier personally framed sacrifice choices and current tiny-risk slider are not direct replications; the new null usefully limits generalization.

Both papers change imagined personal role, but role accessibility, personal safety and stated normative judgments require separate manipulation checks. Assumed equal chances are not automatically displayed task probabilities.
An explicit equal-chance lottery choice differs from midpoint lane positioning that simultaneously minimizes total collisions. These should not be double-counted as the same effect.

The earlier normative analysis makes individual risk and group burden distribution central. This experiment measures public preferences but does not by itself satisfy every affected person's rights or establish universal consent.

deferred.reason: Algorithmic implementation of previously stated principles is proposed, not directly defined/tested as a commitment-device intervention. Read dedicated primary work before adding the broader construct.
A descriptive interpretation of hypothetical risk distribution, overlapping existing self-protection and social-preference entries; no identified unique motive or actual costly act.
Tentative, side-confounded and not robustly detected in the reported treatment regression. Do not add a named bias or normative cyclist priority rule.
Collision avoidance is discussed as an engineering objective, not isolated as a new human/AI behavioral mechanism in this experiment.

limitations: No new entries. One relevant empirical null source and two boundary-only notes improve the existing ontology without increasing the behavior count or inventing annual mentions.
